title: SwiftUI Fundamentals
summary: SwiftUI's declarative model — a View as a pure function of state, and how view identity decides update versus recreate. UIKit interop and deeper state ownership are their own topics.

slides.markdown:
UIKit hands you a view controller and says: mutate this object over time, and remember to keep the view hierarchy in sync with your data yourself. SwiftUI inverts that: you describe **what the UI should look like for the current state**, and the framework figures out what actually changed on screen and updates only that.

The mental shift is the whole framework — a `View` in SwiftUI isn't an object you mutate, it's closer to a formula that gets re-evaluated. Get comfortable with "View is a function of state" and most of SwiftUI's surprising behavior (why a view "resets" sometimes, why `@State` lives outside the struct) stops being surprising.

slides.sectionTitle: Views as a function of state
slides.markdown:
A SwiftUI `View` is a **struct**, not a class, and its `body` is a computed property: `body: some View { ... }`. There is no persistent object holding pixels the way `UIView` does. Every time SwiftUI decides your view needs updating, it calls `body` again and gets back a fresh description of what the UI should look like.

That description is cheap to compute and throw away — SwiftUI diffs it against the previous description and only touches the actual rendered output where something changed. This is why SwiftUI code reads like a spec ("a VStack containing a Text and a Button") rather than a sequence of imperative mutations ("create a label, set its text, add it as a subview").

The consequence: your view struct itself is disposable and re-created constantly. Anything that must survive across those re-creations — state — cannot live as a plain property on the struct; it needs a property wrapper that stores it elsewhere.

slides.sectionTitle: A state change flowing to a re-render
slides.markdown:
When a `@State` property changes, SwiftUI doesn't tear down and rebuild the whole screen — it re-invokes `body` for the affected view, diffs the new description against the rendered tree, and applies a minimal patch to the actual platform views underneath.

![SwiftUI state change flowing through body re-invocation, diffing, and a minimal view patch](assets/swiftui-diff-patch-flow.svg)

slides.subTitle: who owns the source of truth
slides.markdown:
`@State` is for value-type data **owned by one view** — SwiftUI stores it outside the struct's own lifetime, so it survives `body` being recomputed. It should almost always be `private`, because it's meant to be that view's local truth, not something a parent reaches into.

`@Binding` is a two-way reference to state **owned by someone else** — a child view declares `@Binding var isOn: Bool` and the parent passes `$isOn`, the dollar-prefixed projected value that exposes the binding. The child can read and write it, but the actual storage still lives in the parent's `@State`.

The rule that keeps this sane: **exactly one owner per piece of state.** Every other view that needs it gets a `@Binding` (read-write) or is just passed the plain value (read-only). Two views both holding their own `@State` for what should be the same piece of data is the most common SwiftUI state bug — they silently drift out of sync.

slides.subTitle: update in place vs recreate
slides.markdown:
SwiftUI needs to answer a question every re-render: is this the *same* conceptual view as last time (so its `@State` should persist and it should animate smoothly), or is it a *different* view that happens to look similar (so state should reset)?

That answer is **view identity**, and SwiftUI infers it primarily from **structural position** in the view tree — same type, same position among siblings, same loop index or explicit `.id()`. Change the type at a given position (swap a `Text` for an `Image` conditionally) or change an explicit `.id()`, and SwiftUI treats it as a brand-new view: its `@State` resets and it doesn't animate as a transition, it just appears/disappears.

This is why `ForEach` wants a stable, unique identifier per element — reordering a list without stable IDs makes SwiftUI think elements were destroyed and recreated rather than moved, breaking both animations and any per-row `@State`.

slides.sectionTitle: SwiftUI vs UIKit for a new feature
slides.markdown:
| | SwiftUI | UIKit |
|---|---|---|
| Mental model | declarative, state-driven | imperative, callback-driven |
| Boilerplate for a simple screen | low | higher |
| Fine-grained control (custom scroll physics, complex gestures) | improving, still gaps | mature, complete |
| Interop needed with legacy code | via `UIViewRepresentable` | native |
| Team familiarity (most existing iOS codebases) | growing | still the majority |

For a genuinely new screen with no legacy constraints, SwiftUI is usually the right default in 2026 — less code, easier previews, built-in accessibility wins. The real decision point is an existing large UIKit codebase: rewriting a mature, working screen in SwiftUI purely for style points is rarely worth the risk; wrapping SwiftUI for *new* screens inside a UIKit shell usually is.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: mutating state off the main actor

slides.markdown:
Because `body` re-runs on every relevant state change, a single giant `body` that computes a large, complex tree pays that full cost on every change, even a change relevant to one small corner of the screen. Diffing is fast, but not free — a 500-line `body` with heavy conditional logic and expensive computed properties inline can visibly stutter on rapid updates (a scroll offset, a typing field).

The fix is decomposition: break large screens into smaller subviews with their own `body`. This isn't just cosmetic — a smaller view's `body` only re-runs when the state *it* actually reads changes, so isolating a frequently-changing piece of state inside its own small view keeps the expensive parts of the tree from re-evaluating unnecessarily. This is SwiftUI's version of the "don't rebuild the whole tree" performance discipline every declarative UI framework needs.

slides.sectionTitle: The senior nuance: identity is inferred, not declared
slides.markdown:
A junior answer treats SwiftUI's diffing as magic that "just works." A senior answer knows identity is **inferred from structure**, which means innocuous-looking refactors change behavior. Wrapping an existing view in a new container, or switching a `Group { if condition { A() } else { B() } }` to two separate `if`/`else` view builders, can change whether SwiftUI considers a view the same across a state change — silently resetting `@State` that used to persist, or breaking an animation that used to be smooth.

When debugging "my state randomly resets" or "my transition animation snaps instead of animating," the first question is always: did this view's structural position or type actually change between the two states, even if the visual output looks similar? Explicit `.id()` is the escape hatch when you need to force SwiftUI's hand either way — force identity to persist across what would otherwise look like a new view, or force a reset when you deliberately want one (a common pattern for resetting a form when its target model changes).

Deeper state-management patterns — `ObservableObject`, `@Published`, and the newer Observation framework — are covered in the next topic, State Management with Combine and Observation.
